Note about philosophy

Philosophy (mostly, with a bit of religion and science)

For all of my younger years and most of my adulthood my personal inclination was to avoid philosophy and philosophers like the plague. Had it not been that I needed to understand their thoughts for the sake of this book, I certainly wouldn't have troubled to research them. But needs must, so in hope but not expectation I've done some paddling, albeit shallowly, in the turgid waters of the polemicists. For much of this process all those deep, philosophical musings from some of mankind's greatest minds left me cold and unimpressed. It's mostly impenetrable, without some effort and help to untangle, and seemingly self-serving too. Only in the latter stages of my reading about the great philosophers did I begin to realise a little more clearly what they were getting at. It was with this growing understanding that I began to appreciate and admire the amazing thoughts of most of these people.

But it's worth setting out my early, highly critical, reactions of this whole genre because I suspect these are what many people feel about philosophers and philosophy. I had some fun in the process. Here are my initial jaundiced views.

Difficult to understand: Philosophers have a common approach to the way they present their thoughts - with a few exceptions. The more complicated and involved the better, they think. All lengthy philosophical writings are the opposite of the Occam's razor approach, where the simplest explanation is normally the right one. You think I'm being too harsh? Then try out Heidegger: "Temporality temporalises itself fully in each ecstasy, i.e. in the ecstatic unity of the complete temporalising of temporality there is grounded the wholeness of the structural complex of existentiality, factuality and fallenness, which comprises the unity of the care-structure" What...?

Why didn't these great brains apply themselves more productively: dig their garden; concoct a new, nutritious recipe for baked beans on toast; solve both energy and transport problems; come up with a sensible way to prevent Climate Change. They could most usefully even come up with the surest method to stamp out super-bugs, like Covid 19? Instead we have from them diatribes of diarrhoeic output.

Unwise and obvious: Let's have a look back to the beginning, almost, of philosophy's story. We start with Socrates, a giant figure in the early period of Western philosophy. Now he's got a lot to answer for. In Athens, 399 BCE he was charged with mocking the Athenian Gods and of the moral corruption of the city's youth. His sentence, following conviction, required him to swig hemlock. Socrates voluntarily swallowed this nasty poison. The Oracle of Delphi said that there's no wiser man than Socrates. Doesn't sound very wise to me; the nutter. He could have made a run for it. Some Oracle too.

[Figure: Diogenes Sitting in his Tub by Jean-Léon Gérôme (1860)]

Courtesy of Plato, Jean-Leon has a little joke by painting in Diogenes doggy friends, reminding viewers that Plato called Dio a dog. It was Plato who used it as a nickname for Diogenes. Nice one Dio. You should instead be known as the originator of daftism, but maybe I'm barking up the wrong tree and being cynical here. Anyway, the prize for the philosopher with the most unique home, goes to Dio. He takes the biscuit.

Marcus Aurelius, a Roman Emperor no less, did a bit of philosophising in his spare time. He favoured stoicism; a belief that people should accept their lot in life. Marky, I may be overly suspicious here, but it strikes me that the widespread application of this philosophy would have been very convenient to you as Emperor. If you could convince those revolting Huns on your eastern borders to become stoics, then they wouldn't be quite so revolting.

There's Rene Descartes famous line: "I think therefore I am.", or if you want to be a little superior: "Cogito ergo sum" (Latin, the language of the intelligentsia in Rene's time), "Je pense donc je suis" (in Descartes' native tongue). Rene, old chap, does this mean you didn't exist when you were asleep? Dreams are not conscious thought. Another thing Rene, you might have "thought", or is it "lived", again had you seen The Matrix film (with help from Dr Who's Telephone Box). Then again, who, exactly is the "I" Rene? Can you be certain sure?

Karl Marx gave us Dialectical Materialism, for all the use that's been to anyone, particularly to communists of the old USSR. Hume pronounced on scepticism, but he need not have bothered - Richard Wilson gave a much more practical and entertaining demonstration of this ideology with his catch-phrase: "I don't believe it.", in the BBC TV series "One Foot in the Grave" (sorry David, I do in fact have a soft spot for your pragmatic way of thinking).

Kierkegaard gloried as the founder of existentialism - such contrivance. You can live a very full and happy life in complete and blissful ignorance of this slightly tortured concept.

We are told Nietzsche was both a nihilist and an existentialist. Does this mean he was a striker, with an unpronounceable name, who couldn't score goals for Germany, even in extra time? Kant; well his musings were exactly that, a lot of cant: "Ideas do not conform to the external world, but rather the world can be known only insofar as it conforms to the mind's own structure". Not nearly as bad as Heidegger, but edging in that direction.

Egotistical certainty: Of course, these great thinkers were individualists. Most of them admired, or at least were extremely conscious of the weight of their own intellects, which were indeed supremely powerful in relation to those members of the common herd, like me. This meant they tended to say to themselves "I've thought this through with my immense mind; therefore, my conclusions must be superior to everybody else's." With such a scenario, you might think it hard to find any strands of commonality among philosophers to help enlighten on the G issue but, there are a couple of shared threads that have some relevance. For example, many philosophers exhibit an empirical approach that focuses on their own experience and direct knowledge. "If I haven't experienced it, or am unable to conceptualise it directly from my life experiences, then it can't exist." This is the starting point for many (by no means all) of the philosophies that the great thinkers propound. It is the antithesis of Faith which is such a powerful factor in the God debate for those with a religious inclination.

Isimitis: This is a disease any serious philosopher must contract, if he/she wants to be included in the philosophers' Premiership division. They must come out, ideally all over, in an ism. There's Diogenes Cynicism, Plato's Platonism, and Satre's Existentialism, to name but a few.

Common views of philosophy and philosophers: Ordinary people (now there's a statement that could launch a whole flotilla of argumentative philosophy books) may find Ps irritating or baffling. Others (probably quite a lot of them) possibly take a more straightforward and dim view of philosophy and philosophers. They dismiss both as far removed from the real world. Philosophers' prognostications are seen to have no bearing or help with how people live their lives. These sceptics may see Ps philosophising in terms such as:

headings.text: The three Routes to Knowledge and Wisdom

pages.text:
Philosophy: This is a route down which we can travel to learn and understand more about life, the world and everything. Through study of philosophy and by following the rigour of philosophical thinking knowledge and wisdom can be gained apparently, although not necessarily correctly. But, arguably it's only one of three routes to knowledge and wisdom, the other two being religion and science.

Religion in brief

Some people claim that only one of these three routes will lead us to true knowledge. On the other hand, there are sceptics who say we are not capable of knowing true reality; regardless of which route is taken. We cannot be sure of anything at all these doubters assert. We will investigate the reasoning behind such views later, but not now. In this chapter of the book, Hello, Hello, the focus is on philosophy but in other areas of the book religion and science get a much fuller examination. Before focusing on philosophy let's have just a brief look at religion and science and their claims to be, if not the fount of all knowledge, at least the most secure base for true knowledge. Then we will return to philosophy.

Religion: In 1871, British anthropologist Sir Edward Burnett Tylor, defined the essential element of all religion quite simply as: "the belief in spiritual beings." He thought animism was the earliest example of religion. Later Tylor's elegant definition was expanded to recognise that religions commonly have a set of beliefs, rites and rituals specific to the particular religion. These usually fall under the umbrella of a church, which has a structure of expert practitioners who take the lead with the observance of the rites and rituals. They are also authoritative figures who can give answers to theological questions.

Many religions refer to a supernatural entity and a personal God. They typically claim there is a form of afterlife or alternate existence after death. Their beliefs are usually based on a particular holy book. The Abrahamic ones and some others tell of a supernatural basis for creation.

[Figure: Ancient Egyptian artifact]

What's the origin of religion's claim to be the fount of all knowledge? Humans have always had religion of one sort or another, even back to pre-historic times. We know from the evidence of more than 30,000 years ago forms of spiritualism, usually shamanism or animism, were practiced by our hunter-gatherer forbearers.

These early forms of religion, closely identified with the natural and imagined spiritual worlds, had probably been in existence since the dawn of modern humans, around 300,000 years ago.

About 10,000 years ago agricultural societies began to replace hunter-gathering humans. Humans gathered in larger groups and with the more assured food supply that agriculture offered had more time on their hands. They were able to use this spare time to develop more complex religious beliefs. Since the dawn of agriculture religion has grown into a mighty and diverse industry, now dominated by the monotheism of the Abrahamic trio: Christianity, Islam and Judaism. But it also includes many others, predominately far-eastern ones, like Hinduism, Sikhism, Shinto and those that blur the line between religion and philosophy such as Buddhism, Taoism and Confucianism.

These institutionalised religions have in common their certainty of a type of reality. They claim to know how things have worked and will work out, in metaphysical terms, and they tell us of absolute truths, particularly about the consequences of different types of human behaviour and the relevance of good and evil. These religions are largely a form of revelatory knowledge, via various holy texts. It is a matter of faith that the content of the texts was revealed to the author(s) by some great power. The texts give all the necessary answers to how humans should live their lives and in what way the particular deity must be revered. The sacred texts must not be questioned. Believers are required to have faith in place of proof.

The Bible is stuffed full of examples of revelatory truth, one of very many, appropriately towards the beginning of the book, is the story of man's origin. In Genesis, chapter 2, God says: "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, & breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul" (https://www.kingjamesbibleonline.org/1611Genesis-2-7))

We now know, thanks to Charles Darwin and Wallace, that man was the product of evolution. He was not formed out of dust, unless the Biblical author was thinking of stellar dust. Some believers think evolution happened too fast to be natural. It must have been speeded up by God they say. Other believers claim that Genesis is only intended to give a general indication, both of creation and man's original defiance of God. It's not meant to be taken literally.

There have also been several attempted logical proofs of the monotheistic God's existence, but to date no one has yet managed this feat. These are described in detail elsewhere in this book. Nor has anyone shown conclusively that re-incarnation happens or that the state of nirvana can be achieved, as claimed by Buddhism. So perhaps religious revelatory truth is not truth at all. It may either be allegorical, just unsupported opinion, or even simple story telling.

However, many millions believe their brand of religion gives some knowledge about big issues, like the existence of a supreme being, the origin of the universe, man's place in it and what is expected of him. The use of the term "man" is sometimes meant to be generic and include women, although in principle religions women may be a little ignored or treated as less important than men.

Religion therefore is a form of true knowledge for many people. Some believe so fervently that anyone with alternate beliefs can be subject to physical disapproval. The strength and intolerance of religious belief has led to much violent conflict. Charles de Montesquieu, a judge and political philosopher, thought this was the result of narrow-minded bigotry.

"Religious wars are not caused by the fact that there is more than one religion, but by the spirit of intolerance.... the spread of which can only be regarded as the total eclipse of human reason."

Charles de Montesquieu 1689 to 1755

Religion gets a much fuller airing in several other chapters of this book.

Science in brief

Science: Finally, we have science as the third source of knowledge. There are some similarities with philosophy. Both use rigorous argument in support of a particular conclusion. However, science attempts to offer proof though experimental evidence of a key factor. It is absent from the other two disciplines. Science tends to take a step-by-step approach along the route to true knowledge. Often the apparent truth of a previous step is overturned, amended or added to by a later step. It tries to prove its case through reason based on observation, experiment and testing. Statistics and mathematical equations can play a big part in the scientific approach, as can the basic laws of physics and chemistry.

In 2011, at a Herefordshire conference, Professor Stephen Hawking claimed that science was in the lead in the knowledge race: "Scientists have become the bearers of the torch of discovery in our quest for knowledge."

Many scientists express doubt when the question of God and religious beliefs is asked: "If we are honest - and scientists have to be - we must admit that religion is a jumble of false assertions, with no basis in reality." - said Paul Dirac, the great Quantum physicist, of Bristol and Cambridge fame. See more on science in Chapter 24.

Comparative Features of the three roads to knowledge

There are other features to note about the three roads to wisdom. Proponents of one or the other will sometimes champion their knowledge source as the only correct road to follow. Religion does stand out in contrast with the other two here. It is only religious zealots who can sometimes kill, maim or imprison if their religion's version of the truth is not adhered to. Philosophers and scientists are not known to murder in defence of their ideas. They are more likely to dispute verbally or in writing, occasionally very forcefully. Pythagoras was a one-off here. He did break the philosophers duck by drowning a student for giving the game away on irrational numbers. And there is the milder incident where Wittgenstein is alleged to have waved a poker at Karl Popper. These occurrences though fail to get anywhere near religions propensity for murder on a mass scale.

Togetherness: Philosophy, religion and science do not always stand entirely alone, sometimes one route can blur into another. Philosophy is the only one of the three schools that can have strong links to the other two. Religion has been, especially in the past, anti-science to an extent and likewise science can be dismissive of religion. Some philosophers use philosophy to support religion; others see it as a separate, truer basis for knowledge than what they consider to be superstitious religious beliefs. Voltaire dramatically put it: "Superstition sets the whole world in flames; philosophy quenches them."

Another connection - church approval or disapproval: Philosophy is sometimes closely linked to religion because theologians may identify a philosopher's ideas as giving support to their religious beliefs. The two can also be connected for the opposite reason; the church strongly disapproves of a philosopher, and his philosophy.

headings.text: Comparative Features of the three roads to knowledge

pages.text:
He likes it. No he doesn't like it.

Having one's philosophy strongly approved by the dominant church allows a philosopher to get his name and ideas mentioned publicly. Aristotle was much admired by church theologians, mostly up to Galileo (1564-1642), but a bit beyond him too. Aristotle's mistaken view that the Earth was the centre of the universe fitted in nicely with Roman Catholic beliefs for about 2,000 years.

Other philosophers may also get publicity, for the opposite reason. They may be strongly disapproved of by an established religion. Galileo is an example. He daringly went against Catholic certainty by saying the Earth was not the centre of the universe. It was only in 1992, 350 years after Galileo, that Pope John Paul II finally admitted the Catholic Church's condemnation of him had been in error. A couple of hundred years after Galileo, Church creationists were not enamoured of Darwin's evolutionary ideas. For many of them, the Biblical Book of Genesis was believed to be literally true. Spinoza got a huge amount of unintended free advertising. He was excommunicated and declared a non-Jew in 17th century Amsterdam. In addition, his works were banned by the Catholic church. Upsetting two churches did wonders in getting his name and philosophy bandied about. To this day, he is still to the fore because several efforts to have his excommunication rescinded have all failed. Jewish historian, Joseph Klausner tried unsuccessfully in 1927. Other attempts included one in 2012, put before a committee of four, which included the American philosopher Steven Nadler. This resulted in yet another refusal.

Believers and unbelievers comparative intelligence: There have been a number of surveys into the issue of whether there is an inverse relationship between the strength of religious belief and intelligence. In his 2006 book: The God Delusion, Prof. Richard Dawkins said: "Of 43 studies carried out since 1927 on the relationship between religious belief and one's intelligence and/or educational level, all but four found an inverse connection. That is, the higher one's intelligence or education level, the less one is likely to be religious or hold 'beliefs' of any kind."

A 2005 Gallop international study surveyed 50,000 people in over 65 countries. It discovered that people with a higher level of education are less religious than those with either a basic education or no education. Another somewhat similar outcome came from a later study, in 2013. This was by Edward Dutton and Dimitri van der Linden, for Rotterdam University. They concluded that the results showed that on average religious people are less intelligent than atheists. It suggested the reason for this is that religion can be considered instinctive while intelligence is the ability to rise above this instinctive drive. All this is definitely a little unfair on religious people. There are innumerable highly intelligent people, past and present who have had some form of religious belief.

[Figure: Illustration comparing religious vs non-religious child rearing]

Chicago found that children raised in a secular home showed greater awareness and had, in general, a morality based on: "treat others as you would wish to be treated." The study suggested that atheists are better at bringing up their children, partly because the children were more likely to be encouraged to have independent, rational thought. Also revealed was that non-religious people tended not to engage in corporal punishment. This was of course, a generalisation.

Non-G: Child, you are not old enough to understand, this is what you must believe. And you must obey, or else! Be nice to other children.

G: Here are issues about religion, what do you think son, daughter? Think and question, again and again. ?Philosophy?

PHILOSOPHY - definitions, usage and origins

We are now going back to focus on philosophy.

Meaning: What exactly is philosophy? There are a lot of definitions, just try any dictionary or a Google search and you will see what I mean.

The Oxford Dictionary gives one definition: "The study of the fundamental nature of knowledge, reality, and existence, especially when considered as an academic discipline." Not bad, but philosophy covers more than this, as will be explained. The great Plato had a more fundamental description: "Wonder is very much the affection of a philosopher; for there is no other beginning of philosophy than this." Yes, it's possible to wonder about anything. That's at the base of all philosophy.

Plato's brilliantly simple one-word description - wonder - needs to be fleshed out a bit more. It was the ancient Greeks who got philosophy well and truly on the road so it's natural to look to them and their meaning of the term. Not surprisingly they were the first to formally coin the particular words, philo (love) and sophia (wisdom). When joined together these became philosophia meaning the love of wisdom. The term later gained a second and wider meaning; the logical exploration of ideas, virtually on any topic.

Their original definition - love of wisdom - points to the motivation of these Greek philosophers. They wanted to understand and gain knowledge, not just ponder the nature of knowledge.

The later meaning - the logical exploration of ideas - described more specifically what they did and how they did it. A meld of these two meanings is what philosophy is all about in a nutshell. But, given the extent and range of philosophical coverage over more than two and a half thousand years since the Greek originators, that shell comes from one mighty big nut! Philosophy is renowned for its argumentative and contentious nature, so there can be a lot of dispute about this statement.

Is there any point to philosophy?

A fair question. As touched on earlier, you can find lots of people sceptical or even contemptuous of philosophy. They don't see that it has any relevance to their lives. Philosophy can be a complex subject, with its own quite difficult language and sometimes pedantic, tortuous reasoning. It can go into minute and seemingly pointless detail. Bertrand Russell puts it like this:

What is the value of philosophy and why ought it to be studied? It is the more necessary to consider this question, in view of the fact that many men, under the influence of science or practical affairs, are inclined to think philosophy is anything better than innocent but useless trifling, hair-splitting distinction, and controversies on matters concerning which knowledge is impossible.... if the study of philosophy has any value at all...it must be only indirectly, through its effect on the lives of those who study it, it is in these effects therefore.... that the value of philosophy can be sought.

Well, all interesting stuff Bertrand but surely philosophy has more of an impact than simply on the lives of those who study it?

Here's another comment from Bertrand, in its favour, although he may still be thinking only about those who specialise in philosophy:

The point of philosophy is to start with something so simple as not to seem worth stating, and to end with something so paradoxical that no one will believe it.

(Bertrand Russell)

What's it all about?

headings.text: Is there any point to philosophy?

pages.text:
Socrates pared away so finely at every apparent certainty, maybe he reached a level of doubt to an extent he could not be sure he knew anything. Or maybe his was a teasing remark, claiming false modesty. It's perfectly possible, after all Socrates was known to have a sense of humour. He was also well aware that Athenians had high regard for his supreme intelligence.

Aristotle, in one of his many comments about knowing and knowledge said this: "What we know is not capable of being otherwise; of things capable of being otherwise we do not know, when they have passed outside our observation, whether they exist or not. Therefore, the object of knowledge is of necessity." and, "To say of something which is that it is not, or to say of something which is not that it is, is false. However, to say of something which is that it is, or of something which is not that it is not, is true." You have to read this a second time, quite slowly, to appreciate what he's saying. But you may now have reached a stage where you want to close this book and watch some TV. We are starting to get into the area of complexity and nit-picking that makes many turn away from philosophy. However, both Socrates and Aristotle are worthy of noting. They have indicated that the extent of human knowledge is an important issue, so let's carry on. So, back to the first point, ie., what is knowledge? In basic terms knowledge is an understanding of reality. Information of this reality is gained through a process of reason and experience or a combination of the two. For some religious claims of knowledge, it's neither by reason or experience, it's revelatory and faith based.

Traditionally, the type of knowledge we have been concerned with is known as propositional knowledge. This is the knowledge about the result or end point rather than knowledge of how to do something. In arithmetic, we know that 3+4=7. Knowing the answer, 7, is propositional knowledge. The knowledge of the addition process that is needed to arrive at the answer is not propositional. Epistemologists generally concentrate on what they consider to be propositional knowledge. When examining more deeply propositional knowledge, philosophers have come up with two types:

You can spend much time getting more "knowledge", or perhaps more confusion about all this. If you really want to go further take a look at what Hume, Kant, Richard Rorty, Wittgenstein, Russell, Edmund Gettier and Simon Blackburn have said, among others. Then try and de-construct these knowledge related terminologies: constructivism; empiricism; externalism; fallibilism; fideism; foundationalism; historicism; holism; idealism; instrumentalism; logical positivism; nominalism; positivism; rationalism; representationalism; scientism and verificationism. Go into all this detail if you feel inclined, but we are not going any further here, enough is enough. We now deliberate on the main philosophical topic areas.

Metaphysics:

This term comes, yet again, from the ancient Greeks. It simply means beyond or after physics. Specifically, it deals with questions about the nature of reality, e.g. what is existence; what is the cause of existence, sometimes referred to as "being" and "first cause". But since the ancient Greek philosophers, like the pre-Socratics, the scope of metaphysics has widened. It now includes issues of space and time, e.g. is there such a thing as space, and if so does it have infinite size; does time have a beginning and an end?

Other disciplines also attempt to address questions of reality and existence, namely religion and science. Science, as indicated, takes an approach that relies on propositions that can be proven by rigorous experiment and observation, although science has inched towards greater understanding of the answers to metaphysical questions, it has not yet come up with a complete solution. The Great Theory of Everything remains an elusive goal.

As for religion, there is no end of explanations for the origin of existence. The vast range of religious beliefs give different specific answers but have two common, underlying themes. First, nearly all claim the entirety of existence is, down to an eternal God, or Gods. Second, none can offer unchallengeable proof.

Early Greek pre-Socratic philosophers more than 2,400 years ago first considered metaphysical problems, pondered the origin of all matter, and gave their reasoning for various answers.

Political philosophy:

In western politics for example, philosophers like John Locke, Thomas Paine and Karl Marx have had a huge impact. The former two influence the USA's Declaration of Independence document and to some extent the British constitutional model. Jean-Jacques Rousseau's ideas - Liberté, Egalité - were fundamental to the French revolution. The democratic processes inspired by Locke, Paine and Rousseau, with their emphasis on freedom and equality, have been copied throughout the western world.

Marx helped establish the communist system, which is still around, sort of, in China and Cuba. John Adams, the second President of the USA was a great admirer of Cicero's political philosophy. Other philosophers have had a say about politics and been studied by thoughtful politicians such as: Confucius, Thomas Hobbes, Machiavelli, Bacon, Marx and Hannah Arendt. It's fair to say political philosophers have had an impact on the lives of hundreds of millions of people right up to the present day.

"War is politics by other means", said Carl von Clausewitz. This topic may not be something that philosophy can be proud of, ie. giving philosophical pointers to the best way to conduct war. In war situations, some military strategists have probably paid close attention to what Sun Tzu had to say about 2,000 years ago. Basically, his advice was to try diplomacy first and if that doesn't work be ruthless and use overwhelming force to intimidate your opponent into submission. Apart from Sun Tzu, others of the great, famous and not-so-famous have pontificated about war. Aristotle offered some sideways support for Sun Tzu: "We make war that we may live in peace." Much later US General Norman Schwarzkopf fished in the same pond seeking slightly different pisces: "The more you sweat in peace, the less you bleed in war." The devious Nicolai Machiavelli, not surprisingly, gave this advice: "Never attempt to win by force what can be won by deception." All these were saying: "Don't dash to war, try hard to avoid it, peace is better."

Religious Philosophy:

Theologians over the centuries have sought to use the pontifications of philosophers to help give credence to, and prop up their religion. However, they have to be quite selective in which philosophers they choose to support their case. Lots of philosophers do not believe in a deity, or, like Protagoras, say they do not know whether or not Gods exist. Plato and Aristotle were the fond favourites of many theologians, up to at least the middle ages. Both P and A believed we had a soul, as did their great mentor Socrates. Plato's imagined place of Perfect Forms has some similarity to the idea of heaven or paradise. Plato also suggested there should be a perfect, non-physical love. This might have led to the Roman Catholic Church insisting its priests be celibate.

Some philosophers could also be described as theologians - Augustine, Anselm, Aquinas and Averroes particularly.

Ethics and Morals:

These topics are not an exclusive religious preserve. They may be taught to Children by parents at home or in school. Ethics and morals are a major subject for some great philosophers. Ethics comes from the Greek ethos, meaning customs and morals is derived from the Roman moros, also meaning customs.

The Egyptian vizier, Ptah Hotep 4,500 years ago laid down virtuous dictums, focusing on the importance of honesty, openness and, kindness. Some 2,000 years after Ptah the great Socrates was interested in moral issues that affect human lives. In his awkward, questioning way, he would ask a Judge "What is justice." And a Priest would be faced with "What is piety."

To lead a good life, Socrates thought, moral integrity was more important than physical well-being. Many philosophers have made clear their thoughts on ethical issues over the centuries since Socrates' time. They've analysed ethics in so many ways. The result is that ethics is split up into several categories. We have:

Metaethics, this looks at how humans arrive at moral decisions and considers the origin of morality, i.e. can it exist independently of humans? This is an area that interest's theologians. They want to know whether God is the origin of moral standards. One aspect of metaethics is known as Moral or Ethical Rationalism. This claims that general moral principles can be known through reason. Plato and Immanuel Kant were of this view. Later, the idea was rejected, partly, by David Hume and Friedrich Nietzsche. In more recent times some philosophers have backed the a priori concept purported by Plato. This form of ethics, whether called metaethics, moral or ethical rationalism, is more of an investigative, pondering approach. It does not immediately propose necessary action.

Normative ethics, this is a more practical approach than metaethics. It considers what moral standards or rules we should adopt and how these basic standards should be arrived at. It also looks at what our behaviour means for other people. The character excellence sought by Virtue ethics falls under the normative ethics umbrella. This is slightly different to the rules-based approach. Some philosophers think that there are certain defined rules of behaviour that constitutes morality. These behaviours could be basic negatives like "don't steal" or "don't commit murder". However, there are other philosophers who say this approach is too specific and lacks general moral guidance. Aristotle was probably the earliest of this sort. These philosophers support Virtue ethics. For them morality should be broader based and encourage positive good behaviour, like "be kind to others". If you are being kind to others you won't kill them or steal from them. See Bernard Mandeville and his argument that might suggest vice can be a virtue!

Applied ethics scrutinises controversial concerns like abortion; animal rights; human rights; capital punishment; homosexual, lesbian and transgender issues. It also looks at nuclear war - a topic on which the long-lived philosopher Bertrand Russell had something to say. He was strongly against nuclear weapons.

Arguably (anything to do with philosophy is always arguable) the above are the main categories under which ethics is considered. But there is more terminology that is sometimes used to group together theories of ethics. For instance, consequentialism - this simply means that the morally correct action is the one that produces the most good. Bentham's utilitarianism is a form of consequentialism. Then we have deontology. Deontology is nothing to do with teeth, although it does have some bite when it comes to opposing consequentialism. Proponents of deontological ethics say that it's the action itself that must be morally right, not just the outcome. Kant can be seen as a proponent of this concept.

Aesthetics: This is the second strand of axiology, ethics is the first. Aesthetics is also known as the theory of beauty. It explores culture, nature and art generally.

What do Philosophers have in Common?

Philosophers exhibit certain characteristics in common that identify them as a breed apart.

Brilliance: To begin with the great philosophers are all, at the very least, brilliant deep thinkers. Many would be considered geniuses. Look at Thales, he was renowned for his cleverness and identified as one of the Seven Sages of Greece. The oracle of Delphi said there was no wiser man than Socrates. Plato and Aristotle had brains the size of small planets, seemingly (well perhaps not quite, but pretty big to come up with their range and depth of thought).

Know all's: Many philosophers were polymaths, particularly the Islamic Averroes and Avicenna, then we have Leibnitz, Hume, Kant, Russell and Wittgenstein who also cleverly applied themselves to many topics, not just philosophy.

Good at Sums: Mathematical expertise is a factor for some too: Pythagoras, Descartes, Pascal, Leibnitz, Kant, Peirce, Husserl, Frege and Russell especially.

headings.text: What do Philosophers have in Common?

pages.text:
Demanding Home Environment: Another frequent theme in the make-up of these greats was having an influential parent or tortured upbringing; Augustine, Montaigne, Kierkegaard, Locke, Schopenhauer, Wittgenstein (again) are of this type.

Suffering for Their Beliefs: Philosophers are people who, over the centuries, are prepared to come up with original and often controversial ideas. Their expressed views sometimes got them into serious trouble. New ideas might have caused problems for the prevailing religious authorities or were simply disliked by the local rulers. For the offending philosopher often the result was imprisonment, voluntary or involuntary exile. Sometimes their punishment was even worse than these. This treading on of powerful toes, with nasty consequences for the philosopher treader, is a common feature for philosophers. For example, Socrates, Zeno of Elea, Seneca, Cicero and Boethius were either killed or forced to kill themselves. Poor Peter Abelard was castrated, not because of his philosophy, but for his love of Heloise. Galileo initially re-canted his heliocentric views for fear of a spell with the Catholic Inquisition. Some of the unjustly killed philosophers also spent time beforehand in prison. Others were imprisoned but survived: Avicenna; Voltaire and Paine among them. Spinoza escaped prison but was excommunicated because he did not toe the orthodox Jewish line. Exiled philosophers include Aristotle, Diogenes and Hobbes. When they were imprisoned or exiled it gave them plenty of time to focus on their philosophy. This was the same for those who were killed, although the focusing was generally more acute and of shorter duration.

First Letter Influential: Getting off to a good start. It seems that your chances of being recognised as a great philosopher are enhanced if your name begins with letter A: Anaximander; Anaximenes; Antisthenes; Anaxagoras; Aristotle; Aurelius; Augustine; Avicenna; Anselm; Abelard; Averroes; Aquinas; Ayer; Anscombe and Arendt. We also have in the 21st century God's own philosopher, Alvin (Plantinga).

The Laughter and Good Cheer of Philosophers:

It is too strong to say humour is a very common trait in philosophers, but it appears more frequently than might be imagined. Philosophers are generally serious-minded men - mostly men, there are just a few women - who explore serious avenues of thought. Humour is not a known, prevalent factor, but some of the greats did appreciated a joke, and they realised the importance of humour. Socrates was known by Plato to be a convivial and good-humoured man, although no doubt those people he badgered in the Athens market place would describe him less affectionately. Democritus was called the laughing philosopher. He laughed at situations and people, using ridicule and irony.

headings.text: The Laughter and Good Cheer of Philosophers:

pages.text:
There's Augustine's plea to his God not to make him chaste quite yet. Montaigne clearly had a sense of humour saying: "On the highest throne in the world, we still sit only on our own bottom." He also thought cheerfulness went with wisdom and amusingly said: "A life is a fine breakfast, a flat lunch, and a miserable dinner." and "I will never be an old man. To me, old age is always 15 years older than I am." Later than Francis, we have Erasmus who wrote a whole book full of satirical humour.

Likewise, Voltaire with his critical religious parody, Candide. Voltaire also said: "God must have a sense of humour, he invented sex."

John-Paul Sartre showed his sense of humour, saying: "Ah! yes, I know: those who see me rarely trust my word: I must look too intelligent to keep it." Jean-Paul was also the subject of a 1973 comedy sketch by the Monty Python, BBC TV, comedy crew. They acted out a conversation in a launderette between Mrs Premise and Mrs Conclusion. It ends with Mrs Premise telephoning Sartre and asking: "Jean-Paul. Your famous trilogy 'Rues de Liberté', is it an allegory of man's search for commitment?" Jean-Paul: "Oui".

The Monty Python team did several philosophy sketches including The Philosophers Drinking Song. In their version of a Philosophers Football Match, ancient Greeks philosophers are pitted against the German philosophers, with Confucius as referee.

Richard Feynman played the bongo drums for fun. A bongo playing physics genius induces a smile or two. Then we have Arthur Schopenhauer who said: "A sense of humour is the only divine quality of man" An intriguing thought. Did Arthur suggest God enjoyed humour? Ludwig Wittgenstein did not go this far, but he did stress the important place humour could have in philosophy: "A serious and good philosophical work could be written consisting entirely of jokes." and "Never stay up on the barren heights of cleverness, but come down into the green valleys of silliness." Well, I'm trying Ludwig!

The Dalai Lama would agree with Ludwig's underlying assertion that Laughter can be used to embed new ideas. John Cleese, of Monty Python fame (he was Mrs Premise in the Sartre sketch) and much other, interviewed the Dalai Lama about laughter. He asked why it is in Tibetan Buddhism they laugh so often. The Dalai Lama replied that laughter is very useful to him when teaching and in political negotiations. He said that when people laugh, it is easier for them to admit new ideas into their minds. Mark Twain drew this link between philosophy and laughter: "Laughter without a tinge of philosophy is but a sneeze of humour. Genuine humour is replete with wisdom."

Philosophers with religious beliefs

but other philosophers are non-religious.

During the 18th century, the Age of Enlightenment ushered in a new understanding, mostly through the rise of science. This led to a big shift in views, led by Diderot, d'Holbach, David Hume and Nietzsche. In more recent times philosophers who have declared themselves atheist or agnostic of some type include Wittgenstein, Popper, Russell, Singer and Grayling. Then we have the views articulated by that famous group of atheists, Hitchens, Dawkins, Dennett and Harris. These are known as the four horsemen. See them in this YouTube clip discussing the unfair degree of approbation they get as authoritative, atheist authors. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=n7IHU28aR2E

But there are still believers in a God, encouraged partly by the analytic efforts of Alvin Plantinga. He cleverly tried to establish that there is no clear argument against the case for a God. Maybe he was not too successful though. A general survey of 1,972 professional philosophers in 2013 by Bourget and Chalmers found that the vast majority did not believe in God: atheism 72.8%; theism 14.6%; other 12.6%.

In Summary: Regardless of their: mathematical ability; family life; degree of persecution; position in the alphabet; comic facility; beliefs or non-beliefs; the greatest mutual identifying factor, common to all the great philosophers, is an ability to come up with ground-breaking ideas, no matter how much these might be later shot down or amended.

The First Philosophers

It was Pythagoras, 570 BC - 495 BC, who expounded the term philosophia to refer to great thinkers and questioners as philosophers. Of course, Pythagoras is better known to generations of school children for his mathematical skills associated with right-angled triangles. Pythagoras was not the first Greek philosopher, just the first to call himself by that name.

About 2,600 years ago, in the freewheeling Greek coastal town of Miletus (now in Turkey), a man called Thales had new ideas about the nature of all reality. He dismissed the traditional religious views. These claimed everything came from the Gods; the Greek Gods. For Thales, the often cruel, selfish and plain silly antics of Greek anthropomorphic Gods made them unbelievable.

Being a mathematician, he applied rigorous thought to what constituted original matter. According to Thales there must be some basic substance that was the first matter ever to exist. He concluded that everything in nature had water, the Arche, as its base material. His reasoning was that water could be either a liquid, solid or vapour (water, ice or steam). Cicero said that Thales believed it was the mind of a supreme being that created all things from water, if this is so he clearly assumed there was some sort of God.

There are two more important things to note about Thales, his freedom and his school. He lived in a society where it was relatively safe, but not wholly so, to articulate non-conformist ideas. At this time Greece had a democratic government and people were allowed greater freedom of speech, especially if they lived some distance from Athens, as Thales did in Miletus. This freedom was quite unusual compared to many other ancient cultures of his time (although maybe not middle-eastern Akkad where the 2,500-year-old clay Cyrus cylinder suggests religious freedom was allowed).

Thales was not exiled, imprisoned or executed for his anti-religious opinions, as he might have been elsewhere than Greece. He founded the first school of philosophy, later called The Milesian School.

The Milesian School of Philosophy

What is the base substance of everything?

Thales: water
Anaximander: indefinite
Anaximenes: air

Following on from Thales were his pupil Anaximander and then Anaximenes. These two continued wrestling with the metaphysical problem of what was the base substance from which all matter was derived. For Anaximander, it was not water but something indeterminate, which he called the Apeiron and Anaximenes had yet another opinion, it's air he said. These three Milesians did not get it right, but their ideas and freethinking example inspired many others after them.

It's certain that the Milesian school trio got Western philosophy well and truly off the ground. Bertrand Russell says western philosophy began with Thales, but were these the original philosophers on planet Earth? No, they were not. Ptah Hotep, an Egyptian Grand Vizier from some 1,800 years before Thales, deserves that honour. He was the first philosopher that we have evidence of. Ptah wrote ethical philosophical statements. He did not say much though; this may have been because of the limitations posed by needing to have his thoughts chiselled on stone. And, as far as we know, he did not trigger a philosophical movement. Certainly, there is no sure record, on stone or papyrus, of other ancient Egyptian philosophers, although there is a very limited claim made of Imhotep.

But Egypt had an older culture than Greece. We know Thales received some instruction from an Egyptian priest and that he used geometry to measure the height of the pyramids. It's likely therefore he was fully aware of Egyptian mythology. Perhaps he saw the Egyptian Gods in the same dismissive light as the Greek ones and so may have concluded that the Egyptians, for all their sophisticated culture, did not have the answer to the source of reality. He had to work it out for himself.

Other than Ptah Hotep, with his ethical philosophy, there is no one else known to have preceded Thales. In the far east the Chinese Laozi, founder of Taoism, weighed in just a few years after Thales. In India Siddhartha Gautama (Buddha) and back in China, Confucius came slightly later still. However, we are talking about who was the first philosopher in recorded history. By definition, we cannot know of those sages from pre-recorded, i.e. pre-historic times. There must have been some, like the fictional story of Noth the stone-age theologian/philosopher recounted in Chapter 5. However, without written records of some sort, their real thoughts are lost to us.

Philosophy Now

Philosophers and their insights into every aspect of life and beyond have been a part of human culture from Ptah up to the present day. Their many prognostications are outlined in date order in Some Great Philosophers, 104 here. Even given this proven prevalence, at least one eminent scientist has cast doubt over philosophy's continuing relevance.

In 2011 Stephen Hawking said this about philosophy: "Most of us don't worry about these questions most of the time, but almost all of us must sometimes wonder: Why are we here? Where do we come from? Traditionally, these are questions for philosophy, but philosophy is dead." He went on: "Philosophers have not kept up with modern developments in science. Particularly physics."

Physics has not yet answered the questions Stephen posed and philosophy has wider interests than the nature of reality.

Philosophy today is studied at universities and some schools worldwide. Philosophers today remain wide-ranging in their subject matter. Common themes are the philosophy of mind and analytic philosophy. Re the latter, Frege, then Moore and Russell were early proponents. In its initial days it was more associated with language precision - after Wittgenstein. Since then it has developed and tries to take a more scientific, almost mathematical approach to proving or disproving a narrow proposition. Analytic philosophy is popular in the USA and UK. Alvin Plantinga is a leading proponent.

Philosophy of Mind: The issue of mind is not new. Forays into this area, have been made directly or indirectly way back to ancient Greeks. Some of these had a mild look at side issues, loosely connected to the mind. These people were not concerned with the mainly consciousness related questions of the mind which interest's some modern philosophers. The mind interprets our senses and this can result in false or unknown impressions - a sort of unmindfulness maybe? The ancients who took a sideways look at mind include: Plato with his allegory of the Cave; Xenophanes, who in 500 BCE thought knowledge obtained through the senses, and therefore interpreted by the mind, was illusory; then we have Anaxagoras who referred to the natural, directing mind of the cosmos - nous.

"In a sense, then, the philosophy of mind originated together with philosophy itself."

2014, Tiziana Andina (Professor of Philosophy, Turin University)

Wikiquotes

Much later, in the 17th century, Descartes got closer to specific mind philosophical emphasis in saying the mind was separate from the soul - a scenario called dualism.

Socrates (470-399 BC)

[Figure: Portrait bust of Socrates]

1. Socrates (470-399 BC):

Socrates is one of the most famous and important pre-Socratic philosophers. He left no writings, what we know of his philosophy comes through the work of his students, especially Plato.

Socrates' method involved asking questions to help people examine their beliefs and recognize their ignorance. This became known as the Socratic method.

His most famous saying was "I know that I know nothing," expressing intellectual humility.

Socrates was condemned to death by drinking hemlock for allegedly corrupting the youth of Athens and impiety toward the gods.

Plato (428-348 BCE)

[Figure: Portrait bust of Plato]

2. Plato (428-348 BCE):

Plato was a student of Socrates and founded the Academy in Athens, one of the first institutions of higher learning in the Western world.

His philosophy centered on the Theory of Forms, which held that the material world is merely a shadow of a higher reality consisting of perfect, eternal Forms or Ideas.

Plato wrote extensively in the form of dialogues, with Socrates usually as the main character. His most famous work is "The Republic," which discusses justice and the ideal state.

Aristotle (384-322 BCE)

[Figure: Portrait bust of Aristotle]

3. Aristotle (384-322 BCE):

Aristotle was Plato's student but developed his own philosophical system that disagreed with many of Plato's ideas. He founded the Lyceum in Athens.

Unlike Plato, Aristotle believed that knowledge comes from studying the physical world through observation and classification. He made significant contributions to logic, metaphysics, ethics, politics, and natural science.

Aristotle tutored Alexander the Great and his works dominated Western thought for nearly two thousand years.

Confucius (551-479 BCE)

[Figure: Portrait of Confucius]

4. Confucius (551-479 BCE):

Confucius was a Chinese philosopher whose teachings emphasized personal and governmental morality, correctness of social relationships, justice, and sincerity.

His philosophy focused on the importance of:

Family loyalty
Respect for elders
Proper conduct in relationships
Education and self-cultivation
Virtuous leadership

Confucianism became the official state philosophy of China and profoundly influenced East Asian culture.

Lao Tzu (6th century BCE)

[Figure: Illustration related to Lao Tzu]

5. Lao Tzu (6th century BCE):

Lao Tzu is traditionally regarded as the author of the Tao Te Ching and the founder of Taoism (Daoism).

His philosophy emphasized:

Living in harmony with the Tao (the Way)
Wu wei (effortless action or non-action)
Simplicity, patience, and compassion
Natural spontaneity over rigid rules

The historicity of Lao Tzu is debated, and he may have been a legendary figure.

Buddha (Siddhartha Gautama) (c. 563-483 BCE)

[Figure: Image of Buddha statue]

6. Gautama, Siddhartha (Buddha)

Siddhartha Gautama was the founder of Buddhism. He was the original Buddha, Buddha (the awakened one) was born in a wealthy family, wife, not in at a region who are able of having ideas including and discussing his own.

He discovered that suffering is caused through supporting and validating its own views. His teachings emphasized:

The Four Noble Truths
The Eightfold Path
The Middle Way between extreme asceticism and indulgence
Meditation and mindfulness
The end of suffering through enlightenment

Buddhism spread throughout Asia and became one of the world's major religions.

Philosophy of Stoics

7. Philosophy of Stoics

Stoicism was a school of Hellenistic philosophy founded in Athens by Zeno of Citium in the early 3rd century BCE.

The Stoics believed that:

Virtue is the only true good
External things are neither good nor bad
We should focus on what we can control
Reason should govern our emotions
We should accept what happens with equanimity

Famous Stoics included Epictetus, Seneca, and Marcus Aurelius.

Philosophy: how analytic and mind

Descartes

10. Descartes

René Descartes (1596-1650) is often called the father of modern philosophy. He is famous for his method of systematic doubt and his famous statement "Cogito, ergo sum" (I think, therefore I am).

Descartes sought to establish a secure foundation for knowledge by doubting everything that could possibly be doubted. He concluded that the one thing he could not doubt was his own existence as a thinking being.

[Figure: Portrait of Descartes]

John Locke

11. John Locke (1632-1704)

John Locke was an English philosopher and physician regarded as one of the most influential Enlightenment thinkers.

His major contributions include:

Theory of mind as a "blank slate" (tabula rasa)
Empiricist theory of knowledge
Political philosophy emphasizing natural rights
Theory of property
Ideas about religious tolerance

Locke's political philosophy influenced both the American and French Revolutions.

Parmenides of Elea

12. Parmenides of Elea

[Figure: Bust of Parmenides]

Parmenides was another of the first Greek philosophers. He considered the most important pre-Socratic philosophers to be the founder of metaphysics. Parmenides is best known for his radical monism - the belief that reality is one, unchanging, and eternal.

Parmenides argued that:

Change is an illusion
Being is, and non-being is not
The senses deceive us
True knowledge comes through reason alone

His philosophy profoundly influenced Plato and subsequent Western philosophy.

Parmenides' Arguments

13. Arguments

[Figure: Portrait with philosopher]

Parmenides used logical arguments to prove his radical views. His poem "On Nature" laid out his philosophy in verse form.

His student Zeno of Elea created famous paradoxes to defend Parmenides' philosophy, including the paradox of Achilles and the Tortoise.

Democritus

14. Democritus

[Figure: Portrait bust]

Democritus (c. 460-370 BCE) was a Greek philosopher who, along with his teacher Leucippus, developed the atomic theory of the universe.

He proposed that:

All matter is composed of tiny, indivisible particles called atoms
Atoms move through empty space (void)
Different arrangements of atoms create different substances
The soul is also made of atoms

This ancient atomic theory anticipated modern atomic theory by over 2,000 years, though it was based on philosophical reasoning rather than experimental evidence.

Zeno of Elea

15. Zeno of Elea

[Figure: Portrait illustration]

Zeno of Elea (c. 490-430 BCE) was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher and a student of Parmenides. He is best known for his paradoxes, which were designed to defend Parmenides' philosophy.

His most famous paradoxes include:

The Dichotomy: To reach any destination, you must first travel half the distance, then half of the remaining distance, and so on infinitely
Achilles and the Tortoise: Swift Achilles can never catch a slower tortoise in a race if the tortoise has a head start
The Arrow: An arrow in flight is actually motionless at each instant

These paradoxes raised fundamental questions about motion, infinity, and the nature of space and time.

Protagoras

16. Protagoras

Protagoras (c. 490-420 BCE) was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher and one of the first Sophists.

He is famous for his statement "Man is the measure of all things," suggesting that truth and morality are relative to individual or cultural perspectives.

The Sophists were professional teachers who taught rhetoric and argumentation, often for fees. Socrates and Plato criticized them for teaching persuasion without regard for truth.

Philosophers of Stoicism

Philosophers of Stoicism

Stoicism emerged as one of the most influential schools of ancient philosophy.

Marcus Aurelius

Marcus Aurelius (121-180 CE)

[Figure: Portrait bust]

Marcus Aurelius was a Roman Emperor and Stoic philosopher. His personal writings, known as "Meditations," provide insight into Stoic philosophy applied to practical life.

Key themes in his philosophy:

Accept what you cannot control
Focus on your own actions and character
Live in accordance with nature and reason
Practice self-discipline
Remember the transience of all things

Epictetus

Epictetus (c. 50-135 CE)

[Figure: Portrait illustration]

Epictetus was born a slave but became one of the most influential Stoic philosophers. After gaining his freedom, he established his own school of philosophy.

His teachings emphasized:

Distinguishing between what is in our control and what is not
Freedom comes from controlling our judgments and desires
External events cannot harm us; only our judgments about them can
We should focus on developing our character rather than seeking external goods

His student Arrian recorded his teachings in the "Discourses" and the "Enchiridion" (Handbook).

Continental philosophy

Continental philosophy refers to a set of philosophical traditions from continental Europe, particularly France and Germany, that emerged in the 19th and 20th centuries.

Major movements include:

German Idealism
Phenomenology
Existentialism
Hermeneutics
Structuralism
Post-structuralism
Critical Theory

Key figures include Hegel, Nietzsche, Heidegger, Sartre, Foucault, and Derrida.

Continental philosophy often emphasizes:

Historical and cultural context
Interpretation and understanding
Human experience and existence
Critique of reason and society

Id-Great Philosophers

Immanuel Kant

20. Immanuel Kant (1724-1804)

[Figure: Portrait]

Immanuel Kant was a German philosopher who is considered one of the most influential thinkers in the history of Western philosophy.

His major contributions include:

The Critique of Pure Reason, which examined the limits of human knowledge
The categorical imperative as the foundation of ethics
The idea that we cannot know things as they are in themselves (noumena), only as they appear to us (phenomena)
Theory of space and time as forms of intuition

Kant's work created a "Copernican revolution" in philosophy, influencing nearly all subsequent philosophical thought.

Hegel

21. Hegel (1770-1831)

[Figure: Portrait]

Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel was a German philosopher who developed a comprehensive philosophical system known as Hegelian dialectics.

Key aspects of his philosophy:

Reality develops through dialectical process (thesis, antithesis, synthesis)
History progresses toward greater freedom and self-consciousness
The Absolute Spirit realizes itself through history
Philosophy comprehends its own time in thought

Hegel profoundly influenced subsequent philosophy, including Marxism, existentialism, and various forms of idealism.

Friedrich Nietzsche

22. Nietzsche (1844-1900)

[Figure: Portrait]

Friedrich Nietzsche was a German philosopher who challenged the foundations of Christianity and traditional morality.

His key concepts include:

The death of God
The will to power
The Übermensch (overman/superman)
Eternal recurrence
Master and slave morality
Perspectivism

Nietzsche's provocative and often misunderstood philosophy influenced 20th century thought, including existentialism, postmodernism, and psychology.

Søren Kierkegaard

22. Søren Kierkegaard (1813-1855)

[Figure: Portrait with group scene]

Søren Kierkegaard was a Danish philosopher often considered the father of existentialism.

His philosophy emphasized:

Subjective truth and individual existence
The importance of personal choice and commitment
Three stages of life: aesthetic, ethical, religious
The "leap of faith" required for religious belief
Anxiety and despair as fundamental human experiences

Kierkegaard wrote extensively about the nature of faith, the individual's relationship with God, and the limitations of systematic philosophy.

Pyrrhus of Elis

24. Pyrrhus of Elis (360-270 BCE)

[Figure: Portrait bust]

Pyrrhus was the founder of Pyrrhonism, an ancient Greek school of philosophical skepticism.

Pyrrhonism emphasized:

Suspension of judgment (epoché)
Avoiding dogmatic claims about the nature of things
Achieving tranquility (ataraxia) through skepticism
Questioning all claims to knowledge

This philosophical approach influenced later skeptical traditions and continues to be discussed in contemporary epistemology.

Epicurus

25. Epicurus (341 to 271 BCE)

[Figure: Portrait illustration]

Epicurus was born on Samos, part of Greece. He set up a school in the garden of his home, where he taught disciples, including women, children and slaves. This was a highly unusual demonstration of equality for his time. His Epicureanism, Atomism philosophy was mainly about ethics and how people could gain freedom from worry in a state of blissful peace, and aponia, the absence of bodily discomforts and pains.

He lived and taught in his own philosophy. Even as he was painfully dying he wrote a letter: "I have written this letter to you on a happy day to me, which is also the last day of my life... the disease in my bladder and intestines is pursuing its natural course, but against all this is the joy in my heart at the recollection of my past conversations."

His philosophy was summed up by two Greek words: ataraxia, meaning freedom from worry or anxiety; and aponia, the absence of physical pain.

Epicurus's philosophy was mainly about ethics, and how people could find happiness. But the cheerfulness of joy and contentment cannot be emotionally given to suffering. "But the cheerfulness of my mind, the joy I have found in my philosophical contemplation, counterbalances all this," he said.

Zeno of Citium

26. Zeno of Citium (334 to 262 BCE)

[Figure: Portrait bust]

Zeno was the founder of Stoicism and is often confused with Zeno of Elea (who created the famous paradoxes).

Born in Citium (modern-day Cyprus), Zeno came to Athens and studied philosophy there. After studying various schools, he began teaching in the Stoa Poikile (Painted Porch) in Athens - which gave Stoicism its name.

Zeno believed that:

Virtue is the only true good
Living according to nature and reason leads to happiness
We should accept fate with equanimity
Emotions should be governed by reason

His philosophy emphasized logic, physics, and ethics. Following an injury from a fall, it is said that Zeno committed suicide at an advanced age, feeling his time had come. This was consistent with Stoic beliefs about rationally choosing one's end.

Cicero (Marcus Tullius)

27. Cicero (Marcus Tullius) (106 to 43 BCE)

[Figure: Portrait bust]

Cicero was a Roman politician, lawyer, orator, and philosopher. Although he was not an original thinker, he played a crucial role in introducing Greek philosophy to the Roman world.

His contributions include:

Translating Greek philosophical terms into Latin
Making philosophy accessible to educated Romans
Writing influential works on ethics, politics, and rhetoric
Developing natural law theory

His works had immense influence on the Western thought, particularly during the Renaissance. His political philosophy influenced both medieval and Enlightenment political theory.

He was also a great orator and wrote so able to convey convincingly his thoughtfulness and eloquence on in fact, "the many faces of Cicero to different eras to give different perspectives on history on politics on life, on faith and figures, such as David Hume, John Locke, and subsequent Government in Rome and love. He supported the return of a constitutional republic, was a legal theorist and stood out both about the death."

Marcus Aurelius (continued)

28. Marcus Aurelius

[Figure: Portrait bust or illustration]

Marcus Aurelius (121-180 CE) was a Roman Emperor and the last of the "Five Good Emperors." He was also a devoted Stoic philosopher.

His philosophical work "Meditations" was written as personal notes to himself during military campaigns. The work was never intended for publication but has become one of the most important Stoic texts.

Key themes in the Meditations:

Accepting what you cannot change
Focusing on what is within your control
Treating others with kindness and understanding
Remembering the impermanence of all things
Living according to reason and virtue

Despite facing numerous challenges as emperor - including wars, plagues, and political conspiracies - Marcus Aurelius maintained his philosophical equanimity and sense of duty.

Pythagoras (continued)

29. Pythagoras

[Figure: Illustration related to Pythagoras]

Pythagoras (c. 570-495 BCE) founded both a philosophical and religious movement in ancient Greece. Little is known for certain about his life, as no writings of his survive.

Key aspects of Pythagoreanism:

Mathematics as the key to understanding reality
The transmigration of souls (reincarnation)
Vegetarianism and ethical living
The harmony of the cosmos
The mystical significance of numbers

The Pythagoreans believed that numbers were the fundamental reality underlying all things. They discovered mathematical relationships in music and astronomy, seeing the cosmos as an ordered, harmonious system.

The famous Pythagorean theorem in geometry is attributed to Pythagoras, though it may have been discovered by his followers.

Seneca

30. Seneca

[Figure: Portrait or illustration]

Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BCE - 65 CE) was a Roman Stoic philosopher, statesman, and dramatist.

His philosophical works include essays and letters on Stoic themes:

On the Shortness of Life
On Anger
Letters to Lucilius

Key themes in his philosophy:

Making good use of time
Controlling emotions through reason
Accepting fate
Living virtuously
Preparing for death

Seneca served as advisor to Emperor Nero but eventually fell from favor and was ordered to commit suicide, which he did calmly in accordance with Stoic principles.

Ancient Greek Philosophy (continued)

Heraclitus

31. Heraclitus

[Figure: Portrait]

Heraclitus (c. 535-475 BCE) was a pre-Socratic Greek philosopher known for his doctrine that change is central to the universe.

Famous sayings:

"You cannot step into the same river twice"
"Everything flows"
"The way up and the way down are one and the same"

Heraclitus believed that:

Constant change is the fundamental nature of reality
Opposites are unified
Fire is the primary element
The Logos (divine reason) governs all things

His cryptic and paradoxical style earned him the nickname "the obscure" and "the riddler."

Epicurus (continued)

32. Epicurus

[Figure: Portrait]

Epicurus's philosophy emphasized pleasure as the highest good, but he defined pleasure as the absence of pain and disturbance rather than positive sensations.

The Epicurean school promoted:

Simple living
Friendship as essential to happiness
Freedom from fear of gods and death
Moderation in physical pleasures
Intellectual pleasures over physical ones

Epicurus wrote prolifically, but most of his works are lost. His philosophy was later popularized in Rome by the poet Lucretius in "On the Nature of Things."

Augustus (Octavian)

33. Augustus (Octavian)

[Figure: Portrait bust]

Augustus (63 BCE - 14 CE), originally named Octavian, became the first Roman Emperor after the fall of the Roman Republic.

Though not primarily a philosopher, Augustus's reign marked a significant transition in Roman history and provided the political stability that allowed philosophical schools to flourish.

His rule ushered in the Pax Romana (Roman Peace), a period of relative peace and prosperity that lasted for about 200 years. During this time, Stoicism became particularly influential among Roman elites.

Diogenes

34. Diogenes

[Figure: Portrait or illustration]

Diogenes of Sinope (c. 404-323 BCE) was a Greek philosopher and one of the founders of Cynicism.

Famous for his unconventional lifestyle and provocative behavior:

Lived in a large ceramic jar in the marketplace
Carried a lamp in daylight "looking for an honest man"
Criticized social conventions and material possessions
Advocated living according to nature

When Alexander the Great visited him and asked what he could do for him, Diogenes replied, "Stand out of my light."

The Cynics believed in:

Living simply and naturally
Self-sufficiency (autarkeia)
Freedom from social conventions
Virtue through action, not theory

Hypatia

35. Hypatia (c. 360-415 CE)

[Figure: Portrait illustration]

Hypatia was a Greek Alexandrian intellectual, life, Hypatia, is notable as being the first female mathematician and philosopher of significant historical note.

She was head librarian at the Alexandria Library, one of the great libraries of the ancient world.

Hypatia taught:

Mathematics, astronomy, and philosophy
Neoplatonism, a philosophical system combining Platonic ideas with mystical elements

She was renowned for her:

Teaching abilities
Astronomical observations
Commentaries on mathematical works

Hypatia's influence outlived her. Voltaire mentioned Hypatia in his condemnation of the Church and religion. In Charles Kingsley's 19th century novel, she was presented as a Paganfeminist icon. Some see her as the main subject, a well-raised Spanish film about her called "Agora." In 2009, a Hypatia was directed by Alejandro Amenabar with Rachel Weisz playing Hypatia.

Hypatia's life and tragic death have made her an enduring symbol. She was brutally murdered by a Christian mob in 415 CE during a period of religious and political conflict in Alexandria.

Later Western Philosophy

Hipparchia

37. Hipparchia

[Figure: Portrait illustration]

Hipparchia (c. 350-280 BCE) was a Cynic philosopher and one of the first women philosophers.

She married Crates of Thebes, also a Cynic philosopher, and lived according to Cynic principles of simplicity and freedom from social conventions.

Her choice to live as a philosopher was radical for her time, as she rejected traditional female roles and lived openly with her husband practicing philosophy in public.

Boethius

38. Boethius (c. 477-524 CE)

[Figure: Portrait]

Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius was a Roman senator and philosopher who served under Theodoric the Great.

His most famous work, "The Consolation of Philosophy," was written while he was imprisoned awaiting execution on charges of treason.

The Consolation addresses:

The nature of fortune and happiness
The problem of evil
Divine providence
The nature of good and evil

Boethius's work was hugely influential throughout the Middle Ages, bridging ancient philosophy and medieval Christian thought. He translated and commented on Aristotle, making Greek philosophy accessible to the Latin-speaking world.

Augustine

39. Augustine (354-430 CE)

[Figure: Portrait]

Augustine of Hippo was one of the most important Christian philosophers and theologians.

Major contributions:

Synthesis of Christian theology with Platonic philosophy
Theory of time and memory
Original sin and grace
Free will and predestination
City of God vs. City of Man

His works include:

"Confessions" (autobiographical)
"The City of God"
"On Christian Doctrine"

Augustine's influence on Western Christianity and philosophy cannot be overstated. His ideas shaped Christian thought for over a thousand years.

Anselm of Canterbury

40. Anselm (1033-1109)

[Figure: Portrait]

Anselm was a Benedictine monk, philosopher, and theologian who became Archbishop of Canterbury.

He is famous for:

The ontological argument for God's existence
The phrase "faith seeking understanding"
Work on the nature of truth, freedom, and evil

His ontological argument attempts to prove God's existence from the concept of God as "that than which nothing greater can be conceived."

Anselm's work represents an important development in medieval philosophy, attempting to use reason to understand faith.

Avicenna (Ibn Sina)

41. Avicenna (Ibn Sina) (980-1037)

[Figure: Portrait with astrological symbols]

Avicenna was a Persian polymath who made significant contributions to philosophy, medicine, and science during the Islamic Golden Age.

Philosophical contributions:

Synthesis of Aristotelian and Neoplatonic philosophy with Islamic thought
Theory of the soul
Distinction between essence and existence
The "flying man" thought experiment on self-awareness

His medical encyclopedia, "The Canon of Medicine," was used in universities for centuries.

Avicenna's philosophy influenced both Islamic and Christian medieval thought, particularly through his influence on Thomas Aquinas.

Averroes (Ibn Rushd)

42. Averroes (Ibn Rushd) (1126-1198)

[Figure: Portrait]

Averroes was an Andalusian Muslim philosopher, judge, and physician who wrote extensive commentaries on Aristotle.

Key contributions:

Defended philosophy against theological attacks
Argued for the harmony of reason and faith
Commented extensively on Aristotle
Developed theory of the intellect

His commentaries on Aristotle were so influential that he became known simply as "The Commentator" in medieval Europe.

Averroes had enormous influence on European medieval philosophy, particularly at the University of Paris.

Maimonides (Moses ben Maimon)

43. Maimonides (1138-1204)

[Figure: Portrait]

Maimonides was a medieval Jewish philosopher, physician, and legal scholar.

Major works:

"The Guide for the Perplexed" - reconciling philosophy and Jewish theology
"Mishneh Torah" - comprehensive code of Jewish law

Philosophical contributions:

Attempted to harmonize Aristotelian philosophy with Jewish theology
Negative theology - describing God by what He is not
Discussion of prophecy and providence
Rational approach to religious law

Maimonides influenced Jewish, Christian, and Islamic thought. His rational approach to religion made him controversial but also deeply influential.

Thomas Aquinas

44. Thomas Aquinas (1225-1274)

[Figure: Portrait with symbol]

Thomas Aquinas was an Italian Dominican friar and one of the most influential medieval philosophers and theologians.

Major contributions:

Five Ways - five arguments for God's existence
Synthesis of Aristotelian philosophy with Christian theology
Natural law theory
Theory of just war
Analysis of virtues

His masterwork, "Summa Theologica," attempted to provide a comprehensive presentation of Christian theology using Aristotelian philosophical methods.

Aquinas became the official philosopher of the Catholic Church and remains profoundly influential in Christian philosophy and theology.
